findings: PRIMARY OBSERVATION — The two mutating roles are tool-surface-identical, so the code-vs-ops least-privilege boundary is unenforceable where it matters. agents/cto/policy.yaml:33-37 and agents/zeko/policy.yaml:40-44 declare byte-identical tool_filter.allow sets (bash, read, read_image, edit, write, glob, grep, job_kill, job_list, job_output, web_search, skill, exit_plan_mode, todo_write = 14 tools); their deny lists differ only in which sibling each omits. The same identity holds in config/role-preset-mapping.yaml:58-63 vs :75-80 and in the mount-ready drafts config/tool-subagent-instances.yaml (subagent_zeko.allow == subagent_cto.allow; verified programmatically). Because DSH tools.restrict() consumes only allow/deny (role-preset-mapping.yaml:19-31 states 'allow is the primary boundary; deny is the exact-name hard block'), Zeko — whose permissions.yaml row says code_write: no and whose prohibited_actions list code_architecture_change — is granted the full code-mutation surface (edit+write+bash) identical to CTO. The differentiators (capabilities.code_write, prohibited_actions, the 'no code-editing tools beyond scoped ops use of edit/write' note) are advisory control-plane labels that no enforcement layer reads.

Secondary — Nova's deny list is deliberately asymmetric (agents/nova/policy.yaml:40-42 denies only edit, write + 6 siblings; bash and web_search are omitted and rely solely on absence from allow). The note documents this as intentional, but it means deny is not a uniform redundant brake: a future allow-widening for nova would be caught by no deny entry, and tests/validate_config.py:230-231 only checks write/exec tools for roles declaring sandbox: read-only — nova declares sandbox: workspace-write (policy.yaml:30-32), so it escapes that check.

Secondary — job_kill, a state-mutating tool, is in the common allow core of all seven roles, including the strictly read-only reviewer BadSector (policy.yaml:38-43) and the roles whose notes assert 'no execution path' (cfo:36, kai:36). Bounded to session-local jobs, but it contradicts the stated read-only invariant vocabulary.

Positive — The three-way duplication of toolFilter (agents/<id>/policy.yaml ↔ config/role-preset-mapping.yaml ↔ config/tool-subagent-instances.yaml) is already guarded: tests/validate_config.py:220-224 and :290-291 assert mapping==policy and instance==mapping for allow and deny, plus allow∩deny=∅, verified tool names, no delegation tools in allow, and max_depth 1. All seven roles currently pass these comparisons (checked directly: 7/7 MATCH). Drift risk is therefore mitigated; the CTO/Zeko identity is a design gap, not a drift artifact.

risks: Role-separation risk: the ops role holds code-write and bash with no tool-layer distinction from the engineering role, so a mis-routed or prompt-injected task to subagent_zeko mutates source code within its authorized effect scope — least privilege is satisfied at the tool-name layer only in form, not in intent

Silent-widening risk: asymmetric deny semantics (nova) plus a validator that keys its write/exec check on sandbox intent means an allow-list edit for a workspace-write-but-tool-read-only role passes validation unnoticed

Invariant-vocabulary risk: 'read-only' / 'no execution path' claims coexist with job_kill in allow, which weakens the credibility of the invariant set during adversarial review (BadSector) and in audit evidence
Duplication maintenance risk (mitigated today): three files must stay in lockstep per role; the guard exists in tests/validate_config.py but not every consumer runs it before composition

results.recommendation: Before any mount/composition, close the CTO↔Zeko tool-surface identity with a machine-checkable boundary rather than prose: (1) add an explicit toolFilter-level discriminator for the ops role — either drop edit/write from zeko's allow (ops writes are channel/script-routed, and bash remains available for diagnosis) or introduce a path-scoped write predicate if DSH supports one; (2) add a validator assertion in tests/validate_config.py that no two roles' allow sets are equal unless an explicit role_equivalence declaration exists in config/permissions.yaml, and that capabilities.code_write == 'no' implies edit/write ∉ allow for every role regardless of sandbox intent (today that check only fires for sandbox: read-only); (3) normalize the deny convention — either every non-executing role denies bash/edit/write/web_search, or record the 'allow-only boundary' rule as a named invariant so nova's asymmetry is a documented pattern instead of an outlier; (4) move job_kill out of the read-only roles' allow (or document it as session-self-scoped in the invariant vocabulary) so 'no execution path' matches the enforced surface. All four are config/test changes in the control plane; none require authority changes and none were made in this read-only task.
